The moment the orangutan saw it, the animal leaped through the bedroom door, rushed downstairs, and escaped into the street through a window that had unfortunately been left open.

The Frenchman followed desperately. Still holding the razor, the ape sometimes stopped to look back and wave at its pursuer until he almost caught up. Then it ran off again. The chase continued this way for a long time. It was nearly three in the morning, and the streets were completely silent. As the ape passed through an alley behind the Rue Morgue, it noticed light shining from Madame L'Espanaye's open bedroom window on the fourth floor of her house. It rushed toward the building, spotted the lightning rod, and climbed it with astonishing speed. Grabbing the shutter, which lay fully open against the wall, it swung straight onto the bed's headboard. The entire movement took less than a minute. As it entered, the orangutan kicked the shutter back open.

Meanwhile, the sailor felt both pleased and uncertain. He now had a good chance of catching the animal, since it had entered a trap from which it could hardly escape except down the rod, where he could intercept it. On the other hand, he had every reason to fear what it might do inside the house. This fear drove him to keep following. Climbing a lightning rod is easy, especially for a sailor, but when he reached the height of the window, far to his left, he could go no farther. All he could do was lean across and catch a glimpse of the room. What he saw horrified him so much that he nearly lost his grip and fell. It was now that those dreadful screams rang through the night and woke the people living in the Rue Morgue. Madame L'Espanaye and her daughter, both in their nightclothes, had apparently been sorting papers in the iron chest already described. It had been wheeled into the middle of the room and stood open, with its contents lying on the floor beside it. The victims must have been sitting with their backs to the window. Judging by the time between the animal's entrance and the screams, they probably did not notice it immediately. They would naturally have assumed the wind had swung the shutter shut.

As the sailor looked inside, the huge animal had grabbed Madame L'Espanaye by her hair. It was loose because she had been combing it. The ape was waving the razor around her face, copying the movements of a barber.

If I can't live on that, I won't ask anyone to help me out. Is that satisfactory?”

An enormous roar of applause went up. Through it came the king's voice:

“Remove his bonds and set him free! Let everyone honor him, high and low, rich and poor. He has become the king's right-hand man, with power and authority, and his seat shall be on the highest step of the throne! Now sweep away this gathering night. Restore the light and happiness, so the whole world may bless you.”

But I answered:

“It means nothing if an ordinary man is humiliated before the world. But it would dishonor the king if those who saw his minister naked did not also see his dignity restored. May I ask for my clothes to be brought back—”

“They are unsuitable,” the king interrupted. “Bring different clothing. Dress him like a prince!”

My plan worked. I needed to hold things as they were until the eclipse was complete. Otherwise they would start asking me to drive away the darkness again, and of course I couldn't. Sending for clothes bought some time, but not enough. I had to find another excuse. I explained that the king might naturally change his mind and feel some regret about promises made in such excitement. I would therefore allow the darkness to increase a little longer. If, after a reasonable time, he still felt the same, I would dismiss it. Neither the king nor anyone else liked this arrangement, but I had to insist.

While I wrestled with those awkward sixth-century clothes, the sky grew darker and darker, blacker and blacker. At last it was pitch-black. The crowd groaned in terror as cold, strange night breezes swept over them and stars appeared, twinkling overhead. Finally the eclipse was total. I was very glad, though everyone else was miserable, as was perfectly natural. I said:

“The king's silence shows that he still accepts the terms.” Then I raised my hands and held them there for a moment. With the most terrible solemnity, I declared, “Let the spell dissolve and pass away without harm!”

For a moment nothing happened in that deep darkness and silence of the grave. Then, a moment or two later, the sun's silver edge emerged. The gathering let out a tremendous shout and poured toward me like a flood, overwhelming me with blessings and thanks. Clarence certainly wasn't at the back of that flood.

Mrs Clay's feelings had triumphed over her interests, and for the young man's sake she had relinquished the chance of continuing her designs upon Sir Walter. Yet she possesses talents as well as feelings; and it remains uncertain whether his craft or hers will ultimately prevail—whether, having kept her from becoming Sir Walter's wife, he may not in the end be coaxed and fondled into making her the wife of Sir William.

There can be no doubt that Sir Walter and Elizabeth were astonished and humiliated by their companion's departure and the revelation of how she had deceived them. Their illustrious cousins were, of course, available for consolation; but they must long be sensible that flattering and attending upon others, without receiving flattery and attendance in return, affords only half the pleasure.

Anne, convinced very early of Lady Russell's intention to love Captain Wentworth as she should, found her happy expectations clouded only by knowing that she had no relations to offer him whom a sensible man could esteem. In this she felt her disadvantage most acutely. The inequality of their fortunes mattered nothing and occasioned not a moment's regret. But to possess no family capable of receiving him and appreciating him rightly, no respectability, concord, or kindness to give in exchange for the merit and immediate welcome she encountered among his brothers and sisters, caused as sharp a pain as her mind could admit amid circumstances otherwise so full of happiness. She had only two friends in the world to contribute to his circle: Lady Russell and Mrs Smith. To both, however, he was thoroughly inclined to become attached. Despite all Lady Russell's earlier offences, he could now esteem her sincerely. Provided he need not profess to think her right in first separating them, he was willing to say almost anything else to her credit; and Mrs Smith had claims of several sorts to secure his regard both speedily and permanently.

Her recent kindness to Anne would alone have sufficed, and their marriage, far from costing her one friend, gave her two. She was the first to visit them once they were settled; and Captain Wentworth fully repaid every service she had performed, or had ever intended to perform, for his wife. He enabled her to pursue the recovery of her husband's property in the West Indies, wrote on her behalf, acted for her, and guided her through all the minor difficulties of the business with the energy and diligence of a fearless man and a steadfast friend.
